content: The best way to predict the future is to invent it.

attribution: Alan Turing, Computing Machinery and Intelligence
content: We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.
The most damaging phrase in the language is: we've always done it this way.
A ship in port is safe, but that's not what ships are built for.
Simplicity is prerequisite for reliability.
The question of whether a computer can think is no more interesting than the question of whether a submarine can swim.
We are stuck with technology when what we really want is just stuff that works.
Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.
Technology is neither good nor bad; nor is it neutral.
We shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us.
Security is a process, not a product.
The web as I envisaged it, we have not seen it yet. The future is still so much bigger than the past.

attribution: Vannevar Bush, As We May Think
content: The human mind operates by association. With one item in its grasp, it snaps instantly to the next that is suggested.
We have modified our environment so radically that we must now modify ourselves to exist in this new environment.
Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.
Plan to throw one away; you will, anyhow.
All problems in computer science can be solved by another level of indirection.
A distributed system is one in which the failure of a computer you didn't know existed can render your own computer unusable.

attribution: Ken Thompson, Reflections on Trusting Trust
content: You can't trust code that you did not totally create yourself.
Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.
Talk is cheap. Show me the code.
There is no code faster than no code.

A program is read far more often than it is written, so the time spent making it clear is repaid to everyone who comes after, including the person who wrote it and has since forgotten why any of it is there.
Caching is one of the two hard problems in computing, and naming things is the other. The difficulty is never storing the value; it is knowing the moment it stopped being true.
Every abstraction leaks. The point is not to find one that does not, but to choose one whose leaks appear in places you can afford to look at, and to know in advance where those places are.
A backup that has never been restored is not a backup. It is an untested assumption written to disk, and the first time anyone finds out whether it works will be the worst possible moment to learn.

The network is not reliable, latency is not zero, bandwidth is not infinite, and the topology does not stay still. Every distributed system that ignores one of these eventually rediscovers it under load.

Premature optimisation wastes effort, but so does the belief that performance can always be added later. Some decisions about data layout and interface shape are very expensive to reverse once anything depends on them.
Security is a property of a whole system, not a feature bolted to the side of one. A perfect lock on a door in a wall made of paper protects nothing, and most real failures are of that shape.

Version control does not exist to store code. It exists to answer the question of what changed and why, which is the only question that matters when something has broken and nobody remembers touching it.
